items.title: Ted Piltzecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 10, 2019
items.q: I’ve been reading Yuval Harari is this really interesting author who’s getting some attention these days. He wrote a book called Sapiens and followed up with a book called Homo Deus

ctx.x: And I’m wondering, you’re an educator now also. Do you think it’s harder for students these days to be profoundly affected the way you were because there’s so much out there and they have access to almost everything? Does it affect them the way it affected us?

Well it’s a great question, and a profound question because it relates to every aspect of our contemporary culture world wide today. I mean and there are many people that have addressed this: attention span difficulties, you know you can get into anything on a surface level in an instant by just a couple of clicks. And so yes, the answer is I think, unfortunately I do think it’s harder. Yet it’s still happening, it still happens, and there’s a sense of humanity that we all want to hold on to you know. I still…

author who’s getting some attention these days. He wrote a book called Sapiens and followed up with a book called Homo Deus and he talks about the synthesis of technology and biology. And it’s really frightening where it goes. And it does relate to your question because it’s harder and harder to hold on to that sense of what jazz and music represents about our species and our humanity you know, as technology encroaches. And so there are things, you know implants — I don’t mean to get too off the subject here but…
